title: How Many Users Do I Need?
intro: For qualitative work the honest answer is “until new sessions stop changing what we know”. Stakeholders still need a planning number.

topics.title: How Many Users Do I Need?

learn.title: Saturation
learn.text:
Saturation is the point where new data stops changing what you know — **not** everyone saying the same thing, but the core themes holding steady.

Signs you've reached it:

• Repetition across sessions
• Your framework stops changing
• “What surprised me in that last session?” → “Not much”, two or three times running
• Edge cases confirm themes instead of opening new questions

options: New data stops changing what you know
All participants give the same answer
You reach the planned sample size
try.explain: Core themes hold steady; sessions stop reshaping the framework.

learn.title: Planning ranges
learn.text:
Give a range per method and say up front you may stop early or add more:

• Usability test (per group) — **5**, then iterate
• Cognitive walkthrough / think-aloud — **5–8**
• Field / ethnographic — **4–10**
• Concept test — **5–12**
• In-depth interviews — **6–15**
• Diary study — **10–20**
• Qual card sort — **15–30**

Drawn from NN/g, MeasuringU and Sauro. Present them as risk management, not quotas.

try.q: How should a planning range be presented to stakeholders?
options: As the industry standard for that method
try.explain: Say up front you may stop early or add more.

left.label: Treated as a quota
items: Sample size fixed before the question

learn.title: Quantitative starting points
learn.text:
For quantitative questions, the number follows **the claim you want to make**.

From his startup cheat sheet: discovering problems needs far fewer people than estimating a rate, which needs fewer than detecting a small difference between two designs.

So decide the claim first — “we found problems”, “about X% succeed”, “A beats B” — then size for it.

try.q: What determines a quantitative sample size?
options: The claim you want to make
The size of the user base
The number of variants being tested
try.explain: Finding problems, estimating a rate and detecting a difference need very different numbers.

test.q: What is the honest answer to “how many users?” for qual work?
options: Until sessions stop changing what we know
As many as the budget allows
test.explain: Saturation, with a planning range for the calendar.
Agreement isn't the test; a stable framework is. Twice running.

test.q: What is the planning range for in-depth interviews?
test.explain: Drawn from NN/g, MeasuringU and Sauro.

test.q: Where do the ranges come from?
test.explain: Established sources, presented as ranges rather than rules.

test.q: Why five for a usability test?
options: It's enough to find problems, then iterate
Five is the saturation point for all qual work
test.explain: Per group, and then you run another round.
